faq.web.a.danger: I know there are some KiSS implementations which can run in a Web browser by using Web technologies directly, and at the very beginning, I did seriously consider wrapping these KiSS implementations written by others in Electron, but I really dislike writing Electron apps: of course, you can cobble something together by force, but it's really inelegant, and it can't quite give me the UI experience I had in mind (forcing it might work, but I'm afraid it would cost more than implementing KiSS itself, and writing that is boring... I don't want to spend my time on it).

faq.web.tired.danger: I'm also tired of writing lots of disgusting HTML / CSS / JS as a workaround to make a web page pretend to be a native application, and then pack it into a bloated blob of an executable, and of constantly chasing Electron's breaking API changes. On top of that, there's npm, a super uncontrollable thing that makes packaging a hassle and can even get poisoned, and the compatibility between Node versions and Electron versions to deal with (not to mention the versions of each distro)...., and so on and so forth. Taking all of this into account, for a small project like QKiSS, I don't believe at all that developing and maintaining it with Electron or Web technologies would cost less, and I can guarantee that I would have a miserable time developing and maintaining it.

faq.web.chimera.danger: In short, for a desktop application that could obviously be made very lightweight, I have no desire at all to use Electron, a Chimera crossbred from the Web and the desktop.

faq.web.love.danger: Don't get me wrong: I really like Web technologies. Web technologies and Web browsers can do so many things that it's amazing; they're practically one of the greatest engineering miracles of modern human technological civilization. I just think they're a complete mismatch for a use like a KiSS viewer, and for the look of the finished product I had in mind. Just having to carve out, with HTML / CSS / JS, a UI that pretends to be a native desktop application, and carve a file manager into it on top of that, is already unreasonable, while frameworks like Qt have had all of that ready for ages. (Of course, the mismatch and the unreasonableness I mean here only hold as of 2024 at least, when the development of QKiSS began. For the LLMs of 2026, writing this kind of viewer with Web technologies, maybe even with WebGL acceleration + WASM, might take just a day or two...)

faq.web.apps.danger: Besides, Web technologies can of course make amazingly good desktop applications (like VS Code and Figma), but I'm afraid only companies with plenty of development resources, willing to focus seriously on a pile of details, can do that (and clearly, most of them aren't). They also have to know very well what they're doing: the UI flow must be well planned in advance, instead of simply copying the design logic of traditional GUI desktop applications (for example, multiple windows are a very basic UI pattern in traditional GUI applications, but forcing multiple windows in Electron is simply a nightmare: sharing state between windows means IPC, which is fucking hard to write, and maddening... Look closely at software with enough development resources, like VS Code, and you'll see that they too do their best so that you naturally don't feel that sub-windows are missing: for example, the Settings page was made directly as a tab instead of a sub-window, and only around 2026 did it become a modal that looks like a sub-window, but is actually still drawn in the same window; and of course, that modal can't be dragged out of the main window either, since it's just a layer on top of the main window). Otherwise, it's easy to end up feeling that what I'm using is just a program that's sort of like a web page, not a desktop application.

faq.web.landmines.danger: Why am I suddenly rambling so much here? Because before ChatGPT appeared, I developed about five Electron applications, and stepped on quite a few landmines, so I thought I'd mention it while I was at it... Hehe.

If writing this in my free time got me a work injury, there would be no insurance payout.

features.tango-remixer.body.danger: For the 2000s aesthetic romance of Tango-style UI icons, and to bring realistic icons back to a world where flat UIs and monochrome icons, an arbitrary, trend-chasing design fad that never thinks of people with dyslexia, blow around like an ill wind*2, I ended up making the Tango Remixer project on the side, so I could easily stuff Tango icons into Qt projects like QKiSS and keep their look consistent across platforms; then I also took on maintaining three XDG-compatible icon theme packs from the 2000s. Then my OCD couldn't stand making the app public before its icons were pretty, so it took one more year...

features.footnote.browsers.danger: Oh Firefox, what on earth is wrong with you, insisting on removing a pile of icons from the UI? Did it never occur to you that people with dyslexia quite likely use a UI by relying on “position → icon color → icon details → and only then the text”? Making the icons monochrome wasn't enough, and now you've removed them altogether. Even Chrome and Edge, two rogues who don't care whether their users live or die, do a little better than you on this: at least they kept the icons in their application menu. On icons, DuckDuckGo Browser actually does the best job. As far as I know, DuckDuckGo is currently (as of October 2026) the only mainstream browser that still keeps icons in its right-click context menu, crushing Firefox, Chrome, Edge, Vivaldi and Brave, every single one of them. And the icons of its settings screen are even in color! Do you know how excited I was to see that!

faq.winsign.a.danger: Because I didn't pay Microsoft protection money for a code signing certificate.

faq.winsign.how.danger: Simply put, “buying a signature” means: I'm a developer, and once I have written my program, I pay protection money to the Microsoft family itself (or one of its crews), they send their boys to dig up everything about me, and then they put my public key into a public certificate and issue it to me. Then I can digitally sign the compiled executables with my own private key, so that any Windows computer can use the public certificate to verify that “this executable was released by me, signed with my private key, and not by someone pretending to be me”. Indirectly, it also implies that “there is no malware hidden inside” (because once malware is found in it, they revoke the certificate, and since they already have my name, phone number, address, date of birth, ID number, blood type and star sign, they can come to my door any time and fit me for a pair of concrete shoes).

faq.winsign.why.danger: But I don't use Windows in daily life at all: I only use it to play video games. So I have no interest at all in buying a signature from Microsoft. Still, the whole compiling and building process of the software is transparent: you can check it yourself on GitHub Actions.

faq.banana.prepear.danger: Because I don't want a Prepear incident of my own (the case record at the US Patent and Trademark Office). I don't know what's wrong with Apple, but it is super eager to do this kind of thing: maybe its lawyers want to hit their KPIs, or maybe its managers want to show that they are doing something.

faq.banana.tyrant.danger: Before I read that line, I never imagined that capitalists could push people around even here. If they could, they would probably love to register Isaac Newton's half-length portrait as a corporate trademark too, and then charge royalties on every physics textbook.*1

faq.banana.fairuse.danger: Under the nominative fair use of trademark law, you may mention someone else's trademark to say that your product works with theirs, but only “as much as is reasonably necessary”. So I may only write plain text like “macOS”, because in theory that is already enough to say what it means, and I can't add an Apple icon to it. But my OCD makes me feel uncomfortable all over without a little icon for decoration, and since they pick on even images of a “real apple”, I had to think of something else.

faq.banana.ai.danger: My spare time for this project is precious. I don't want to spend a single moment of my life drawing an icon by hand, only for salaried lawyers to make me take it down and redraw it, for some bullshit reason invented by the unreasonable whims of a big corporation. But I can't accept the ugly-as-sin plain “macOS” wordmark they require in its place, either. For something this stupid, it's enough to let AI scribble a rough draft (any fruit will do, as long as its shape has nothing to do with an apple's, so that not even a one-year-old would be misled), then touch it up a little myself. Anyway, the 2013 Mac Pro is the urn that holds the remains of Apple's aesthetics.

faq.banana.footnote.danger: Actually, Microsoft has similar rules too: you may not use or change the Windows logo. But at least they aren't crazy enough to ban even “real windows”, and I've never heard of them going after the icons that developers use on their web pages only to show that something is for Windows. When they did act, it was always against names that clash with “Windows”: for example, Lindows, which was clearly trying to sound like Windows, or (my guess) Windows Commander (now Total Commander), which could be mistaken for an official Microsoft product.

faq.macsign.a.danger: This is also about buying a signatureprotection money, and it works much like the warning on Windows. I don't buy one because it means paying Apple protection money every year for the Apple Developer Program.

faq.macsign.why.danger: But first, I stopped being a Mac user long ago; second, I don't make a living from the Mac or iOS; third, I'm only developing a free software project that I like and give away at no cost, and its source code and build process are all public, right there. So there is no reason at all, and I'm in no mood, to spend 99 dollars every year feeding this ugly, greedy corporation that wants to control even the ways you pay.

faq.macsign.bugs.danger: Besides, for an OS whose obvious UI bugs can sit there for years without being fixed, I don't want to spend a cent on a signature from its vendor. The same money donated to KDE is worth far, far more to human progress.

faq.macsign.musing.danger: Looking back, Mac OS 9.2.2 hardly had any bugs, apart from its poor memory safety, and I used it for years. But around 2016–2018, after a bit over a year with macOS, I got so angry that I installed Linux: through three macOS upgrades, piles of stupid bugs that badly hurt everyday use were never fixed. I really have no idea what they are paid for.
